_note: Newest first. The top version must match MARKETING_VERSION in project.yml (tools/check_content.py checks). 1.0.0 is the App Store release.

releases.title: Tidy hero
notes: The Character screen's gear slots sit in a ring around your hero with more room between them. Your level and EXP moved into the Stats section, and Attack, Defense, Magic and Speed each have an icon, with all the numbers in one size.

releases.title: First come, first served
notes: In a fight, your side acts first, in the order everyone chose their move: choose quickly and you go before your friends, and your companion always goes right after you. The monsters go after your side, the faster ones earlier more often.

releases.title: Your turn
notes: In a fight, the ring under whoever you're choosing a move for (your hero, then your companion) lights up and glows, so it's clear whose turn it is.

releases.title: Road closed
notes: A road a quest hasn't opened yet is fenced off with pickets that follow the line across it, like the town fences, instead of a jumble of upright fence pieces, and its “Closed” sign floats clear of a town's gate arch.
A skill's element badge in battle stays on one line, as wide as its name, instead of wrapping when the row is crowded.
A crowded fight (friends, their companions and a full pack of monsters) shrinks everyone a little and opens a gap between the two sides, so nobody's name plate sits on someone else's head.
Out on the roads, no tree or bush grows right in front of someone you can talk to, so they're never hidden. A boss like the Emerald Dragon gets a wider clearing.
The rewards after a fight fade out at the bottom only when there's more to scroll to, and the fade goes once you reach the end. The scroll bar runs down the window's right edge.
A poisoned fighter shows just the purple drop by their HP bar, without a count of rounds left beside it.

releases.title: Lined up
notes: On the map, your hero's window and the minimap line up along the top of the screen.
The Character screen's stats are bigger and easier to read: taller HP and MP bars, and larger Attack, Defense, Magic and Speed.
Windows opened over the menu (equipment, items) dim the whole screen from the start as they pop in, instead of their shade growing from the middle.

releases.title: Sunrise behind the leaf
notes: The sun rays on the title and loading screens always fan out from right behind the logo's leaf, on every phone and held either way; on the travel card, from behind the swirl.
Hard fights leave Seal Stones: beat monsters 5 or more levels above you (when the tougher battle music plays) and you may win one, better and likelier the harder the fight. A boss always leaves one.
Your hero's looks are chosen once, when you start a new game, and every hair colour and outfit is open from the start: the Character screen no longer has Customize, and quests no longer unlock looks.
Titles are badges of honour now: bronze, silver, gold, ruby, and a shining prismatic badge for the rarest, on the Character screen, in Titles, on profiles and in their colour over names on the map.

releases.title: Buttons at the bottom
notes: On the title screen, Settings, How to play and What's new sit at the bottom of the screen.
What's new's gold dot sits on the edge of its button.
With more than one game, the heroes on either side fade out toward the carousel's edges instead of being cut off.
Your companion on the title screen is no longer cut off at its feet when it squishes or sways.
In a fight, the line of what just happened sits level with the chat button.
Who goes first in a fight is shuffled every round: anyone can open a round, but faster fighters still go earlier more often, so speed still counts.
Gloves, necklaces and boots have slots of their own next to your weapon, armour and accessory: five of each from level 1 up, in town shops and dropped by monsters. Speed Boots are boots now.
The Character screen shows your hero in the middle with what they wear around them; tap a slot to change it. A gold dot marks an empty slot you have something for.
When a fight's rewards don't all fit, their bottom fades out so it's clear there's more to scroll to.

releases.title: A Storyleaf swirl
notes: The swirl where you tap the ground is Storyleaf's leaf green with a dark green outline, so it stands out on every map, from snow and sand to dark woods.

releases.title: The clock waits for the monsters
notes: A fight's time to choose starts once everyone has marched onto the field, not while the monsters are still walking in.
Upright, the monsters stand centred across the screen however many there are, instead of bunched up on the left.
Your and your companion's faces are gone from a fight's top left (HP and MP show on the fighters themselves), so what just happened sits at the top in the middle.
Travelling to another map shows Storyleaf's sky, a leaf-green swirl and the place's name on a cream pill, with the same loading bar as the game's start.
A Homeward Feather whisks you away: feathers whirl up round you as you rise into a column of light, and you float down in it at the other end.

releases.title: Poison and ice all at once
notes: When several fighters are poisoned, the poison bites them all at the same time at the end of the round, instead of one after another. Everyone frozen shivers at the start of the round together, too.

releases.title: No picking when there's only one
notes: With one monster left, Attack, a spell on a monster and Capture go straight for it, without asking which one. The same goes for an item or a healing spell when you're the only one it can help.

releases.title: Capture shows a Seal Stone
notes: The Capture button in a fight shows the Seal Stone you throw, instead of a heart that looked like healing. How to play shows it too.
How to play lights one tip at a time: in town, Towns as you walk into the square, then Quests when Elder Oak speaks. Every tip's highlight is the same width.

releases.title: A softer level-up glow
notes: The rays behind the level medal glow softly and fade out sooner, instead of standing out sharply against the window's blue.

releases.title: Side by side with your companion
notes: In a fight without a friend, you and your companion stand side by side in one line, instead of your companion standing behind you. With friends, companions still stand a row behind whoever they came with. How to play shows it too.

releases.title: A smoother How to play
notes: In How to play's fight, the message line stays in full view once the buttons come up, and a new message takes the old one's place instead of the two blurring together.
In the story's pictures of Meadowbrook's square, Elder Oak stands lower, so his gold ! and his greeting fit above him.
Your companion's name no longer prints over yours when it stands right behind you. It shows whenever there's room for both.

releases.title: Title bars with a clear edge
notes: Window title bars, and the menu's row of tabs, keep their light blue down to a crisp dark edge, instead of fading into the window below.

releases.title: A calmer battle screen
notes: In a fight, your face and your companion's sit top left with their HP and MP, as on the map, and the chat sits top right. What just happened is one slim line under them, or between them on a phone held sideways.

Skills, Capture and More sit on an arc around Attack, all within easy reach of your thumb, and the time to choose drains in a ring around Attack. While a list of skills or items is open, the clock sits on top of it.
The 1× and AUTO buttons moved behind More, as Pace and Auto, and Settings has both switches under Battle. While Auto plays, Attack's corner turns gold: tap it to take over.
On a phone held sideways, a big wave stands a little closer together, so its back row stays clear of the top of the screen.

releases.title: What's new in pages
notes: What's new shows five releases at a time, newest first: Newer and Older under the notes turn the pages.

releases.title: A close button on every window
notes: Every window now has the orange close button in its top-right corner, like the menu and the map: the results after a fight, a boss's story, a full party, a level-up, a finished quest, the tour, a piece of gear's card and the story pages. On the title screen, Settings and making a hero get a title bar with it, like What's new.

What closing does: after a fight or a quest it's Continue, a level-up keeps your points for later, and with a full party it keeps your party as it is (the newcomer goes back to the wild). On the story pages before a new game, it takes you back to the title screen.

releases.title: Less at once
notes: The Character tab has smaller tabs of its own, like Quests: Hero (your stats and gear), Skills and Titles. Skills shows the next two skills your class unlocks, the rest a tap away, and wears a gold dot when you have a point to spend.
Companions and the Monster Book sit on the same smaller tabs. The long explanations on Companions and Friends fold away under How it works once you have companions or friends.
The Bag shows one line per item: tap one for its card, with everything about it. Shops show two lines at most. In Settings, your language is one line, and Change opens the list.
On a phone held sideways, the title screen sits in the middle of the screen, the logo on the left and the rest on the right, for Settings, What's new, the languages and making a hero too.

releases.title: One row along the top in battle
notes: In a fight, the 1× and AUTO buttons now sit just left of the message bar at the top, and the chat button just right of it: one row, all the same height. The waves and the time to choose stay under the message.

releases.title: Quests in two tabs
notes: The Quests tab has two smaller tabs of its own: Quests, for the ones people have given you, and Daily challenges, for the day's bounties, their bonus and your daily gift. When the other tab has something to hand in or claim, it wears a gold dot.

releases.title: One kind of window, and Use in the Bag
notes: Every window and dialog has the same frame now, running all the way round with its title bar or tabs inside it: the menu, the map, chat, trades, shops and talks, item cards, battle lists and results.

Items in the Bag have one Use button (Give for toys). A window then asks who gets it: you or any of your companions, not only the one following you, with their HP and MP, and those it wouldn't help faded.
A quest in the Quests tab opens like a drawer, the rows below sliding along, instead of fading in.

Change on the Character tab now opens a window with everything you have for that slot in a grid, what you're wearing first and pieces you can't use yet faded. Tap one to see its card, then Equip it or Cancel (Unequip for what you're wearing).

releases.title: A tab for your friends
notes: Party & friends has a tab of its own in the menu now, next to Companions: everyone you've befriended, who's in your party, and the Invite and Leave buttons. The Companions tab is just your companions.

releases.title: A tidier title screen
notes: The title screen shows less at once: Continue and New game up front, and Settings, How to play and What's new as small round buttons underneath. What's new wears a gold dot when there are notes you haven't read.
Before your first game, the title screen also offers the language and Import a backup; once you have a game, both are in Settings.
The loading screen's bar is shorter, with a little more room under the logo.
On a phone held sideways, the title screen fits without scrolling: the logo and the round buttons on the left, your game with Continue and New game on the right.

releases.title: Tidier battle buttons
notes: Skills can't be pinned beside Attack any more: the battle buttons are back to Attack, Skills and More, and the Skills list has no stars. Capture still joins them when you can befriend a monster, and Items when someone is low on HP.

releases.title: Seal Stones of every kind
notes: Four new Seal Stones, each in its own colour: the blue Moon Seal holds a monster half as often again as a plain Seal Stone, the pink Heart Seal twice as often and the golden Star Seal three times. Moon Seals are sold in Prismhaven and Larkspur, Heart Seals in Larkspur and Ingothold, and bosses now and then drop a Star Seal.

The rainbow Wishing Seal never fails on a monster that can be befriended. It's very rare: Elder Oak gives you one for the new quest Wish Upon a Star (befriend three more monsters), bosses drop one now and then, and the Monster Book's last reward holds one.

Every throw now uses the stone up, whether it holds or not. While you aim, each monster shows your odds with that stone. Capture throws your plainest stone; choose a stronger one from Items. The first quest gives five Seal Stones instead of three, and the daily gift, the bounty bonus and the Monster Book's rewards hold the new stones too.

releases.title: Monster cards and toys
notes: Every monster has a card now. Beaten monsters leave theirs now and then, rare ones and bosses more often, and each new kind goes in your Monster Book and makes you stronger for good: Fire and Metal cards raise attack, Dark magic, Earth defence, Water speed, Wood HP and Light MP, more from stronger monsters. Spares are sold on the spot.

Toys for your companions: a Tin Soldier, Toy Blocks, a Music Box, a Bouncy Ball, a Cuddly Bear and a Bubble Wand, each raising one of a companion's stats for good, up to ten toys a companion. Prismhaven Market sells them, and bosses sometimes drop one.
Tilly the Toymaker in Prismhaven wants to see your cards: five quests, from five kinds of card to a hundred, each paying in toys. Three new titles for collecting cards, too.

releases.title: A tidier world map
notes: On the world map, every place sits right on its crossroads, and a closed road's lock sits in its middle. The map's window matches the others, and tapping a place tells you about it.

releases.title: Storyleaf's own sky
notes: The title and loading screens wear Storyleaf's colours: the app icon's sky, lavender to mint with sun rays and clouds, and a leaf-green loading bar.

releases.title: Seal Stones for any monster
notes: Throw a Seal Stone at any monster, at any HP, even with others still standing: the weaker it is, the better the odds. Seal Stones are in the battle's Items list too, your companion and friends leave the monster you're sealing alone, and a sealed monster is yours however the fight ends.
With your phone on its side, the world map, the level-up card, an item's details and the Party full! card fit on the screen: what doesn't fit scrolls, instead of running off the top and bottom.
The world map opens centred on where you are, the places along its edges show whole, and the first-play tour's notes keep clear of the Dynamic Island.

releases.title: Richer sound, shorter nights
notes: New sound effects with more depth: fuller hits, ringing bells and a touch of room around every sound. Each element's spells sound like themselves, strong skills gather with a swell of sound, and a mastered skill opens with a grand chord.
In Settings, music, sound effects and footsteps each have their own switch, and a switch that's off is easy to see.
Night passes in about eight minutes instead of twelve, and rain and thunderstorms blow over in about a minute.
The Character tab shows your hero holding their weapon, and a speech bubble's tail now joins the bubble cleanly.

Larkspur has grown: a second ring of streets, many more houses, a windmill and a wizard's tower on the terrace, a fountain on the square, and gardens of lilac and blossom with bird baths for its bluebirds.
In every town, the healer, the shopkeeper and the other townsfolk no longer stand hidden inside or behind a house.
Day and night, and the weather, each have a switch in Settings: off, it's always daytime, or the sky stays clear.
An adventurer's card fits Befriend, Trade and Duel on one line, without the note underneath.
The marks for raised and lowered stats in a fight, and poison's drop, are glossier and a little smaller.
The minimap always shows the colours of the map you're on, even just after arriving from a map that looks different.
Whirlwind spins your fighter round on the spot, a pirouette, instead of tipping them head over heels.
The big blurry trees and bushes that drifted across the screen on some maps are gone: they looked like smudges on the glass.

releases.title: Cleaner buttons
notes: The light buttons lost the stray dark line just inside their top edge. Their shadow now falls only underneath, where it belongs.

releases.title: Quests worth the trip
notes: Quests show what they pay up front, in the Quests list and when they're offered to you: gold, EXP and items, no tap needed.
Quest gold and EXP grow with your level, to a bit more than a daily bounty pays, so an old quest is still worth the trip.

releases.title: Brighter battles
notes: Special attacks land in a flare of light: a bloom, a streak across it, a star of beams and a burst of sparks, growing with the skill's level, so a mastered spell lands like a small sun.
Damage shows with a minus now, like -100, so it reads apart from healing's +100.
New pixel-art icons on the battle buttons, the map's buttons and the menu tabs, drawn like the items.
Friends walking with your party no longer show their titles, so the names over the party don't pile up.

releases.title: Something every day
notes: Titles to earn, 32 of them: for levels, lands, the Monster Book, quests, bosses, friends and more. Wear one over your name from Character → Titles. Other adventurers wear theirs too.
Daily bounties in the Quests tab: three small jobs a day, matched to your level, with a bonus for finishing them all. And a gift each day you play, in a round of seven.
The Monster Book pays out as it fills: rewards at 10, 25, 50 and 75 kinds of monster, and a big one for all of them.
Rebirth is worth more: a fifth more EXP in battle for each one (up to double), titles, and a new colour for your name.

Gentler first fights: Sunny Meadow's monsters are levels 1 to 4, one or two at a time, Windswept Downs' are 3 to 10, and Pineapple Harvest waits for level 8. Frost Breath freezes now and then instead of every time.
Choose how long you get to pick a move in Settings → Battle: off, 10, 20 or 30 seconds. With VoiceOver or Switch Control on, there's no clock at all.

releases.title: How to play, played
notes: The story's pictures are made from the game itself now: real maps with their people and creatures, each boss on the battle stage over its own land, and Meadowbrook's square, where Elder Oak greets you.

How to play plays the game: the joystick and a tap walk you along a road, a fight with the real buttons, Fire Bolt and your companion's Pine Needles, a Seal Stone sealing a monster, LEVEL UP! with the victory card, and a quest in town. Each tip lights up while its part plays; tap a tip to see its part.
A fight no longer freezes for good when you tap AUTO while the battle buttons wiggle to be rearranged. A beaten boss always drops its gear again, even when its followers dropped two pieces first.
Capture waits for a boss's last wave: a monster sealed in an earlier one was lost, Seal Stone and all, if you then fell or ran.

Music comes back by itself after a call, Siri or an alarm, and when you switch to headphones or a speaker. Your saved games' dates and your starting hero name follow the language you chose, and so do the phone's own screens, like the Files picker for backups.
Villagers' names are translated now, like everyone else's.

releases.title: A bigger bookmark
notes: The app icon and title logo have a slightly smaller storybook leaf with a softer shine and a wider red bookmark, so it reads clearly on your home screen.

releases.title: More life on the maps
notes: New little animals live on the maps: songbirds hop and peck about and fly off when you come close (then land back once you've gone), chicks wander the towns, squirrels bound through the woods, lizards scurry over the sand and mice patter about the caves. Butterflies flutter in Prismhaven, Larkspur and Lotus Land too.

The darker, harder places have creepier company: red-eyed crows that flap off as you pass, spiders and rats skittering about the caves, scorpions in the sand and will-o'-wisps glowing in the swamps, haunted hills and temples.

releases.title: Cleaner battle marks
notes: The blue and crimson arrows by a fighter's HP bar no longer have a number beside them: an arrow up means a stat is raised, an arrow down that one is lowered. Poison still counts down its rounds.

releases.title: The fight waits for you
notes: Leave the app in the middle of a battle (another app, the lock screen, a call) and the turn timer stops where it was. It picks up again when you come back, so you don't lose your turn.

releases.title: Who's about
notes: The minimap shows the other players on your map as dots: blue for adventurers, white for friends you've made, red for red-named ones looking for a fight, and green for friends in your party. In dark caves you only see those standing somewhere you've already lit.

releases.title: Waking up in town
notes: When you faint, you wake up in the last town you visited, not at the edge of the map where you fell, so a zone that's too hard for you can't keep knocking you down at its entrance.
Won fights now and then leave a Homeward Feather, and a beaten boss always does, so a long trip out always has a way home.

releases.title: A way home for everyone
notes: Homeward Feathers are on sale in every town shop for 50 gold. Use one from your bag outside battle and the wind carries you back to your checkpoint, like the Mage's Bridge of Light, whatever your class.

releases.title: Fresh strength with every level
notes: Levelling up fills your HP and MP again, and your companion's when it levels up too. Between fights your wounds still stay with you.

releases.title: Purple poison
notes: Poison is purple now, from the cloud and bubbles to Venom Bite, Poison Mist and the drop by the HP bar, and a curse turns crimson so the two never look alike. The poison and curse marks sit in front of the HP and MP bars instead of half hidden behind them.

releases.title: Welcome to Storyleaf
notes: The game has a new name: Storyleaf. The goddess Liora binds the world's tales into one great book, and its pages are the land you walk. A new logo and app icon come with it: a leaf that's also a storybook.

Towns, lands, people, bosses and quests have new names of their own: Prismhaven, Larkspur and Ingothold, Gumdrop Peaks, Marionette Rise, Dozywick, Moonwhisper and more. Your hero, bag and progress carry over as they were.

releases.title: Your wounds stay with you
notes: A level-up no longer refills your HP and MP, or your companion's. You leave a fight with the health it left you, so drink a potion, use a healing skill or rest at the healer before the next one.
Other adventurers' companions now suit their level: a seasoned mage walks a monster from the far lands they've travelled, not a starter bunny.
Friends in your party keep their HP and MP between fights too. Their own heals carry over, and the healer rests them along with you; one who faints wakes up bruised, at half strength.
Frost Breath freezes its targets solid: whoever it catches loses their next turn, you included.
Accessories drop far more often: one piece of gear in three that a monster drops is a ring, a charm or boots, and they keep dropping from the toughest monsters too.
The orange arrows that mark who you can target sit over the monsters again; when a boss wave marched in, they were left hanging at the top of the screen.

releases.title: A Seal Stone that seals
notes: Catching a companion looks like sealing now, not throwing a ball: the teal Seal Stone from your bag floats over the monster, a glowing seal opens on the ground beneath it, and the monster turns to light and spirals up into the crystal. The crystal pulses, lighting the seal's marks one by one, until it shines gold, or cracks apart and the monster pours back out.

releases.title: Two genders, every hairstyle for everyone
notes: Heroes are male or female now; the Other option is gone. A hero who picked it keeps their race's original look and can choose again in Customize.

Every hairstyle suits everyone: a boy can wear a ponytail or braids and a girl spiky or swept hair. The Bob, Shoulder and Messy styles stay too, for every race and gender. Each gender still starts with its own hair, first in the list.

releases.title: Storyleaf in your language, and a story told in pictures
notes: Storyleaf now speaks eleven languages: English, Spanish, Portuguese (Brazil), French, German, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese (Simplified and Traditional). Everything is translated: menus, battles, chat, quests, dialogue, monster lore and these notes.
Pick your language with the globe button on the title screen, or under Language in Settings. It switches at once. Until you choose, the game follows your phone's language when it has it.

The story at the start comes to life: three chapters, each with a little animated scene from the game. Liora gathers the tales into one land, the Big Bad Wolf, the Rat King and the Drunk Dragon loom out of the dark, and you walk into Meadowbrook with your companion while Elder Oak waits. How to play now acts out a fight, right up to a Seal Stone catching a jelly.

releases.title: Bigger boss waves
notes: Boss fights are a real battle now: every wave brings 10 monsters, in two rows of five. The waves before the boss are ten of the map's own monsters, and in the last one the boss stands in the middle of the back row, behind nine of its followers. The early waves are weaker to make up for it: the first stands about 13 to 20 levels below the boss and the second 7 to 14 below, while the boss's own followers stay close to its level.

releases.title: Day, night and weather
notes: The world follows the clock now: the light warms at dawn and dusk, and at night the maps sink into deep blue. The sun's glow and its beams fade as it sets and come back in the morning. Caves stay as dark as ever.

Weather comes and goes, changing every few in-game hours: cloudy skies, rain with ripples on the ground, storms with lightning, banks of fog and snow flurries. Each place has its own: the swamp and the dark woods are often foggy and wet, the desert is nearly always clear, snowy lands get fresh snow and the shores the odd storm.
The game's own notices about sunrise and sunset now say Storyleaf, like everywhere else.

releases.title: A look for every skill, and bots that think
notes: Every skill now has a look of its own. Frost Breath is an icy breath that grows crystals of ice and drifts snow, no longer Bubble's water orb; Bubble sends a stream of bubbles that pop. Ember sprays little embers, Mud Shot lobs a gob that splats, Rock Throw hurls a tumbling boulder, Vine Whip lashes, Golden Spin flings a spinning gold disc, Gust blows streaks of wind, Roar sends out shockwaves, and Web Shot throws webs. Bash slams down from above, Shadow Bite and Venom Bite bite in violet and green, Evil Eye opens a great glaring eye, Poison Mist rolls in as a fog, and Flash bursts into a blinding star.

Heals and buffs too: First Aid raises a white cross, Recovery a beating heart, Mend Beast paw prints, Blessing a rain of light; Protection forms a shield, Holy Glow an orb of rosy light, Guardianship a dome over the party, Animal Training paw prints and speed lines, Boost rising arrows and Berserk red flames.

Friends no longer copy you. They weigh every move: a plain blow to finish off a monster rather than spending MP, a sweep when there's a crowd, a spell where it hits a weak spot and never where it's resisted, their best skill on the toughest monster, a heal or a buff when it pays, and MP kept back if they're the healer. They rarely use the skill you just used, and on Auto you fight the same thoughtful way.

releases.title: One spacing for both sides
notes: In battle, your line and the monsters' are spaced alike: five of yours stand exactly as far apart as five monsters, and every other line in the fight follows the same spacing. It's the widest that still fits the most crowded line, a companion at its end included.

releases.title: Spells that raise you up
notes: New spells raise stats for a while: Protection for Fighters (an ally's DEF +40%, from level 12), Holy Glow (an ally's MAG +30%, level 40) and Guardianship (the whole party's DEF +20%, level 60) for Mages, and Animal Training for Beast Tamers (ATK +20% and SPD +30%, level 25). They grow stronger with their skill level, and Bless now raises ATK and DEF the same way.
Whenever a spell raises or lowers a stat, the fighter shows which and by how much ("DEF +40%" in blue, "ATK −20%" in violet), and an arrow by their HP bar counts the rounds it has left.
A curse now lowers ATK and MAG, shown on the cursed fighter, and poison's bite each round is marked "Poison" so you can see what took the HP.

Some monsters power themselves up now: golden hamsters, wood hogs, blaze bulls and earth lions Boost their ATK, and werewolves, fire bears and shadow apes go Berserk (more ATK, less DEF). Companions of those kinds do it for you, and friends cast their buffs on whoever they'd help most.

When a friend or your companion goes up a level with a win, light pours down on them on the field with "LEVEL UP!", and the victory card lists them. Friends now keep pace in the same win you level up in, if they were still standing.
What's new: only the newest release is open; tap any other to read it.

releases.title: A proper speech bubble
notes: When you talk to someone, the window's tail is part of the bubble now: the glass and the light-blue border run out round it, where it used to be a dark triangle stuck over the border. It points at the speaker's face instead of their chest.

releases.title: Spells of light
notes: The elemental spells are drawn in light and colour like the rest of the battle's effects, no more pixel art, and each glows in its own element's colours: Fire Bolt and Ember are a blazing orange fireball that bursts into flame, Jelly Splash, Bubble and Frost Breath a blue orb that splashes into a crown of droplets, Leaf Storm and Vine Whip a cyclone of green light, and Stone Spike, Mud Shot and Rock Throw shards of ochre light bursting out of glowing ground.
Every glow keeps its colour on bright ground too: a soft tint of the element's deep shade sits under the light, so the desert doesn't wash it out to white.

releases.title: Tap a monster to attack
notes: Attack is already chosen when your turn starts, and your companion's: tap a monster and you attack it, no Attack button first. Pick a skill, an item or Capture to do something else instead.

releases.title: Armed friends, a tidy line, honest roads
notes: Your friends and the other adventurers hold a weapon for their class and level, on the map and in battle, and their card shows what they hold and wear.
Friends and companions walking behind you show their walk the whole way instead of sliding along.
In battle, your line stays evenly spaced and now spreads across the screen: it only keeps room at the end for a companion when there is one.

The world map shows quest gates the way the game has them: a road is dashed with a lock at the end it's closed from, and it's open coming the other way. Tap a place to read which road is closed and which quest opens it.

releases.title: A slimmer turn clock
notes: The clock under the battle log is narrower, so it no longer reaches over the 1× and AUTO buttons.

releases.title: No more houses on the roads
notes: Some houses in Ingothold, Prismhaven and Meadowbrook stood right on a street, blocking it. Each has moved to the nearest clear plot beside the road, most of them a step or three. Meadowbrook's windmill and Prismhaven's guild hall stay on their terraces, just off the street that leads up to them.

releases.title: Railings that follow the terraces
notes: The stone railings along the raised terraces in Meadowbrook, Prismhaven, Ingothold and Larkspur run along the terrace edges at the map's angle, as one railing, instead of stepping down them like stairs.

releases.title: Gear from battles
notes: Monsters drop equipment now: weapons, armour and accessories from up to their own level, mostly for your class. Stronger fights pay better: a monster at your level drops a piece 6% of the time, ten levels above you 16%, well below you 2%. A rare monster drops one a third of the time, and a boss always does, on top of its own rare drops. Two pieces at most a fight.
How many you have of an item shows as a small blue badge on its picture: in your bag, on the Character tab, in battle's item list and in what a win turned up.

releases.title: Fire looks like fire
notes: Fire's badge has a new flame with three tongues. The old one was a teardrop, and on the small badges it looked just like water's droplet. The fire skills' buttons show the new flame too.

releases.title: Back up your game
notes: Settings has a Back up to Files button: it saves your game as a file in Files or iCloud Drive. Bring it back with Import a backup on the title screen, on a new phone or after deleting the app. It comes back as a game of its own and never overwrites another.
Your games were already in your phone's own iCloud Backup; this is a copy you keep yourself.

releases.title: Faster fights, and Auto
notes: A 2× button at the top left of every fight plays it twice as fast. Your 10 seconds to choose stay the same. It's kept for the next fights.

Auto, next to it, fights for you against monsters at least 5 levels below you: your hero does what a friend would (wake a fallen friend, heal one in trouble, or go for the weakest monster, now and then with a skill), and your companion fights on its own. It stays on from fight to fight until you switch it off, hands back to you when you're badly hurt, and never plays in a boss fight or a duel.

releases.title: Friends can join again
notes: Inviting a friend to your party no longer crashes the game. Since 0.3.21 every invite did, whatever the size of your party: up to four friends and their companions can travel with you, ten of you in all.

releases.title: No take-backs
notes: Once you've chosen what you do in a fight, that's that: your companion's turn no longer has a button back to your own choice, which also started your clock over.

releases.title: Dressed for their level
notes: Other adventurers wear armour now, like players would: what their class can wear at their level, mostly the best of it. Chain mail, plate, robes, jackets, ranger cloaks, dragon mail and snow cloaks, and speed boots on some, where before everyone wore the same tunic. Your party friends dress up too, and their gear gets better as they level with you.
Towns are full of adventurers about your level instead of beginners, each with a class and the gear to match, and with all sorts of hairstyles.
Monsters knocked out by the same blow fall together, with one line for all of them ("Jelly ×2 and Fire Rat are defeated!"), so a sweep that wins the fight doesn't wait on each one in turn.

releases.title: Caves stay dark in a fight
notes: In Rat Cavern, Gooey Grotto and Whispering Hollow a fight keeps your light: behind the fighters the cave is lit only as far as it reached, and the rest stays dark, so a battle shows no more of the cave than your light does.

releases.title: Bots' hair, every shade
notes: Other adventurers' hair takes its colour on every shade, like yours: no more red strands and outlines in black, blue or white hair, in town, in your party, in battle and on their cards.

releases.title: Companions behind their owners
notes: In battle every companion stands right behind the one it came with: yours behind you, each friend's behind that friend, a rival's behind the rival. The people stand in front, however small the party.

releases.title: Ten seconds to choose
notes: Battles give you 10 seconds to choose each turn instead of 5, and your companion gets its own 10 when you command it. When the bar runs out you still attack the monster you last hit.

releases.title: A busier world
notes: Every computer-run adventurer wears a BOT tag: over their head, in the chat, on their card and stats, and in your friends list.

Towns are busier: Meadowbrook has twice the adventurers it had, and Prismhaven and Larkspur 14 each instead of 8. Ingothold's main square is a market: traders stand about under signs showing what they sell today, call out their deals in the chat, and trade with you when you walk up.

The chat has announcements on a gold banner: dawn and dusk, a word when you arrive somewhere, news of other adventurers, and rare monster sightings. A sighting is real: for 20 minutes that rare monster turns up far more often on its map.

releases.title: Fainting splits the party
notes: When you faint, a fight isn't over while a friend is still standing: they fight on without you, and a friend who knows Revive wakes you up, you first. It's lost once nobody's left standing (your companion doesn't fight on alone).

Whoever is down when the fight ends wakes up at their own checkpoint. You wake at yours, even if your friends won, and get no EXP from that fight, like a fainted companion. A friend who fainted wakes at theirs: the last checkpoint they reached with you.

Friends still standing when you fell wait for you where the fight was. They stay in your party but sit out fights, greyed out in the top-left corner, and their stats say where they are. Walk up to them and they set off with you again.

releases.title: A clearer stats window
notes: The stats window's numbers are white, so attack, defense, magic and speed stand out on the dark window (they came out dark there).
Skills show as their icons with names under them, your gear as item pictures, and a friend's companion with its picture, level and element gem.

releases.title: See anyone's stats
notes: Tap someone on the map to see their stats: an adventurer, a friend travelling with you, a friend's companion, or your own companion. The faces in the top-left corner open them too, yours included.

The window shows their level, race and class (or species and element), HP and MP, attack, defense, magic and speed, and their skills, with your gear and EXP on your own and a friend's companion on theirs.

releases.title: Bosses fight in waves
notes: A boss fight comes in three waves. Its followers come at you first, two of the area's monsters at a time, and the boss steps forward with the third wave, in the middle of its last two followers.
Your HP and MP carry over from wave to wave, so pace your skills and potions. Each wave stands a few levels closer to the boss's, and the boss always has the highest level on the field.
A tracker under the battle message shows which wave you're on, with a star for the boss's. Every monster you beat pays out at the end, the boss's waves included.

releases.title: Fairer bosses, and fixes from a full playtest
notes: Revive works: fainted friends show as ghosts while you choose who to wake, and tapping one casts it. Before, they had faded away and couldn't be picked.
Beating a boss always counts as a win. Its last minion no longer runs off at the end, which turned the win into "It got away…" with no story, no rare drop, and the boss still waiting for you.
The Gilded Brute, the Howlmaster and the Marionette King had stats meant for bosses 20 to 50 levels higher. They're now as tough as the bosses around them, and pay like them.
Bosses fight with their own element: the Wavecrest Dragon blows bubbles, the Craghulk slings mud, the Emerald Dragon lashes vines and Morvane bites with shadow, instead of all of them breathing fire.
Mages learn Fire Bolt when they join the guild at level 10 (Recovery moves to 15), so a new Mage has a spell to fight with.

Eleven side quests, from Lost Little Lambs to Stardust's Night Flight, were offered long before you could face their monsters. They now open at the level of the place they send you: the Frog Prince's at 21, Puss in Boots at 55, Night Flight at 85.
Companions and friends hold back from a weakened monster only on the round you throw a Seal Stone at it. Before, just carrying a stone made the whole party stand around while the monster got away.
Friends heal with their best healing skill, not always First Aid. Poison, curses and Bless end when a fighter faints, so a revived one starts clean.
Only your hero's and bosses' mastered skills get the big golden show, so fights with a full party don't drag.

The Bag no longer lets you drink a Seal Stone: only potions and ethers have Hero and companion buttons, and nothing is used up when it wouldn't help. Hatching an egg with five companions says there's no room.
Spare gear shows how many you have (×2) in the Bag and the Change list. Reborn heroes no longer see the skills they know listed again as locked.

The Companions tab and the Monster Book say where your first egg comes from and that befriending needs a Seal Stone. The first-play tour no longer mentions a "P" bar, and a boss you've beaten no longer answers taps on the spot where it stood.

releases.title: Elements you can read at a glance
notes: Elements show their shape on a glossy gem of their colour, not just a coloured dot: a flame for fire, a droplet for water, a leaf for wood, a mountain for earth, a magnet for metal, the sun for light and the moon for dark (neutral is a dashed ring). Light, metal and neutral are gold, silver and pearl, with their shape engraved. The gems mark each monster in the Monster Book and its element filters, and every element tag on skills, companions and monster pages.

releases.title: A livelier world
notes: Gumdrop Peaks is made of candy now: a pink sugar path, milk-chocolate ponds, groves of cotton-candy trees in lemon, peach and sky blue, giant lollipops in five flavours and presents in the grass, with candy sprinkles drifting down.

New things to find: candy canes, gumdrops, giant cupcakes and gingerbread houses on Gumdrop Peaks; paper lanterns and mochi in Moonwhisper; marionettes, toy blocks and jack-in-the-boxes on Marionette Rise; a sleeping cat and big pillows in Dozywick; flying carpets floating over the Genie Desert and the Hidden Steppe, with genie lamps; poppy fields on Emerald Road; giant ladybugs in Lotus Land; garden gnomes, scarecrows and bird baths in the meadows; treasure chests and messages in bottles on the beaches; and apple trees in the Smiling Forest, along Emerald Road and in the Snow White Forest, frosted blue there.

Little animals live on the maps: bunnies in the meadows and forests (the snowy ones too), frogs by the ponds of Frog Swamp, Lotus Land, Swan Lake and Twilight Woods, and crabs on the beaches. They hop about, and hop off when you come close.
Now and then birds fly over the meadows and towns, gulls over the beaches and lakes, and bats over Shiverdell, the Big Bad Wolf's Lair and Marionette Rise, their shadows sweeping over the ground.

More in the air: dandelion fluff over the grasslands, bubbles rising in Frog Swamp, Lotus Land and the Tidewater Shrine, paper lanterns floating up over Moonwhisper, sleepy Z's over Dozywick and music-box notes over Marionette Rise. Magic lanterns and star crystals bob gently where they float.

releases.title: Bosses with a story
notes: Boss fights happen right where you stand, with the map behind them like any battle, and a boss brings two of the area's own monsters along, a little weaker than itself, standing at its sides.

The first time you beat a boss, a short story tells what the win means: who's free again, which road opens, who'll want to hear about it, and where the trail leads next. Bosses you've beaten keep their story in the Monster Book, so you can read the ones you won before this update too.
The Earth Snake is brown all over now, without the green that showed through on its coils, and the Light Snake is the pale, glassy gold its description promises instead of salmon and olive.

Monsters wear the colours their names promise. About two dozen colour variants came out another colour: the Azure Golden Hamster was mint, the Crimson Yellow Butterfly blue, the Rosy Wood Crab olive and the Frosted Phantom olive green, while the Amber Werewolf and the Violet Black Lizard barely differed from the usual kind. Each is the colour it's named for now, from the Sunny Fire Rat to the Shadow Blaze Bull, and keeps its shading's warm highlights and cool shadows instead of one flat colour.

Recoloured scenery keeps its shading too: autumn trees go red in the shadows and gold on top, and red maples catch orange light. A house's wooden door no longer takes the colour of its roof, mushroom houses keep their beige stems, the yellow and blue daisies lose their pink streaks, and Lotus Land's path is sandy again instead of green.

Your companion takes orders: after you choose your own move, choose its: Attack, one of its skills, Guard, or Auto to let it decide. It gets its own 5 seconds, and fights on its own when they run out. Rather it fought alone? Turn off "Choose your companion's moves" in Settings.

Curses and poison, Storyleaf's dark arts: a poisoned fighter loses HP at the end of every round for 3 rounds, and a cursed one hits 20% weaker for 3 rounds. A green drop or a violet arrow by the HP bar shows the rounds left. Mages learn Curse at level 12 and Poison at 25. Watch out for the Venom Bite of snakes and widows, the Poison Skeleton's Poison Mist, and the Evil Eye of phantoms and Morvane.

Bigger parties: up to four friends can travel with you now, a party of five, and they bring their companions. Each companion walks at its friend's side, fights beside them, and shows next to them in the Companions list. In battle a party of more than five stands with the people in front and the companions in a row behind. A friend who's around while your party is full says so instead of showing nothing.

A fainted companion's card no longer says it's following you: it says it can't follow you or fight until it's healed, with a button to give it a potion from your bag. In battle, friends' companions carry their owner's name ("Sprout's Water Slug"), so they're never mistaken for yours.
In portrait battles, people stand in profile as they do in landscape: your party looks left toward the monsters instead of showing you their backs.
The level badge on a fighter's bars now sits centred against both the HP and the MP bar, not just the HP bar.

Fixed your games list filling up with copies of one hero: the save from before you could keep several games was copied in again whenever the title screen opened, and Continue could pick up an old copy. It moves in once now, the untouched copies are cleared away (any you played on are kept, and can be deleted in Settings), and each game shows when you last played it.

releases.title: Spells that land
notes: Stone Spike bursts out of the ground in real rock: the earth cracks, shaded spikes shoot up round the target (tall ones behind, short ones in front), throwing rocks and dust and knocking it off its feet, then sink back. The more you train it, the more spikes, up to a giant one at the top.

Fire Bolt is a flickering fireball trailing embers that bursts into a blast, burns out into smoke and scorches the ground. Stronger casts set flames licking round the target and send a column of fire up through it.
Leaf Storm whips leaves, and petals as it grows, into a cyclone round every foe, passing in front of them and behind with gusts of wind.
Monsters' water spells (Bubble, Jelly Splash, Frost Breath) lob a wobbling orb of water that bursts in a splash and a spray of drops.
Mastered spells finish with the new art too: a rain of fireball meteors, a forest of stone spikes, a hurricane of leaves.

With three or more of you travelling together, the faces in the top left fold into one row of small faces under yours (your companion's with its HP), so they no longer cover the map. Tap the row to see everyone in full, and the arrow to fold it again.
Beat another adventurer in a duel, or one who picks a fight with you, and they drop everything they carry: the goods they'd have sold you that day go into your bag.
While you talk to someone (or trade, chat or open a menu), the joystick and the buttons step aside instead of peeking out from behind the conversation.

Your companion and friends no longer walk through water or cave walls: where there's no room beside you, they fall in behind you in single file, in your footsteps. Adventurers' pets keep to dry land too.
Caves are dark now: you see as far as your light reaches, a warm circle round you that flickers like a flame, and beyond it the dark. Glowing crystals and moss still shine faintly through it.
In a cave the minimap shows only what your light has fallen on, so you map it as you go instead of seeing every passage from the start. What you've explored is saved.

Battles keep moving: you have 5 seconds to choose each turn, counting down in a bar under the battle log. When it runs out you attack, going for the monster you last hit (or the first one standing). The clock waits while the chat is open or you're moving the buttons around.

releases.title: Hair that fits
notes: Each gender keeps its own hair: a female human's ponytail, an Other human's bob, a male elf's swept hair, an Other elf's shoulder-length hair, a female dwarf's braids and an Other dwarf's messy mop are the styles they start with, and theirs alone. Picking another style no longer leaves the old locks and braids hanging.

Every hairstyle sits right on every head: an elf's ears poke through instead of stretching into wings, no stray ear tips or collar bits ride along, and a style takes your race's own hair colour (blonde on an elf) until you dye it.
Dyeing your hair no longer dyes your boots, belt and cuffs.

Tap an item when trading, in a shop or at the smith to see all about it: who can use it and from what level, its stats against what you're wearing, and what a material forges into. Gear you couldn't use says why right in the list (Beast Tamers only, Needs level 30).

releases.title: Every hair
notes: Dyeing your hair now colours all of it. The darker and redder strands at the edges kept their ginger before, and so did much of an elf's long hair; now every shade takes the new colour.
Hair that falls over the shoulders, side locks and beards (a female dwarf's long hair, a male elf's beard) take the colour too.
Changing your gear: Unequip now sits beside the item you're wearing, Done closes the list from below it, and the items to choose from line up with the one you're wearing.
Skills on the Character screen show their MP after the name, like Bash (12 MP), with the mastery bar at the right end of the row.
The coins next to your gold on the calendar plate are easy to see: a deeper gold with a dark edge, as big as the sun and moon.
In battle every ground circle is seen from the same angle (heroes stood on flatter circles than monsters), and both sides line up at the same slope however many fight on each side.

Levelling up is a big moment now: light pours down on your hero and LEVEL UP! fills the battlefield with the jingle, then the victory card (and the quest card) shows your new level on a gold medal with the stats it raised.

releases.title: Rare finds
notes: Six rare monsters that never turned up now do: the Azure Golden Hamster and Starry Hedgehog on the Windswept Downs, the Rosy Wood Crab and Frosted Mud Eagle on Pineapple Shore, the Crimson Yellow Butterfly in Lotus Land and the Amber Werewolf in Big Bad Wolf's Lair. The Monster Book can be filled at last.
A companion or friend who goes on guard in battle really does take half damage for the rest of the round, like you do.
The Companions page gives the real capture rule: weaken the last wild monster standing to 20% HP or less (it used to say half).

releases.title: Face forward
notes: Female humans, male elves and female dwarves (and the other body type) showed the back of their head in the round portrait top-left and in other pictures facing you. They face you now.
While you wear armour, Customize leaves out the Outfit section entirely instead of explaining why it can't be changed.
In battle the monsters and your party stand further apart, so the two sides read as lines facing off instead of a crowd.
The items you find after a battle (or get from a quest) sit centred on the card.
The Monster Book no longer says Light and Dark monsters are both strong against and weak to each other: it says they hit each other extra hard.
You can chat during a fight: the Chat button sits under the battle log on the right.
The world map opens centred on where you are, instead of on the middle of the map with your town cut off at the edge.

Mastered skills (yours, your party's and bosses') put on a real show: the battlefield dims, a magic circle and a pillar of light rise under the caster, and the skill ends in a finale in its own element: a meteor rain, a tidal wave, a forest of stone spikes, a leaf hurricane, pillars of holy light, a tornado or giant crossing blades.

Everyone fights in their own style. Fighters close in with a double slash, mages stay back and fire a bolt of magic from a rune circle, beast tamers pounce with claw marks. Before a skill, a mage draws a rune circle, a fighter flares up in a battle aura and a tamer calls a swirl of wild spirits. Elves dart in quicker and shed leaves, dwarves hit hard enough to shake the ground.
A friend in your party brings their companion into battle too.
Skill names in battle no longer show the skill's level (Lv 7): just the name.

releases.title: Dressed for battle
notes: While you wear armour, Customize no longer offers outfit colours: the armour decides how your clothes look. Take it off to dye your clothes again.
Levelling up no longer opens the skill card when every skill you know is mastered and there's nothing new to learn; points are kept for the next skill your class unlocks.
Shops buy too: tap Sell in any shop to sell materials and gear you've outgrown for half their price.
Trade with adventurers you meet: tap Trade on their card. They pay half again what a shop would for things they want, and sell a few things of their own. Offers change every in-game day.

Skills take 10 steps to master instead of 5, each step a little stronger (a mastered skill still hits 80% harder than a new one). Your progress carries over: a skill at level 3 is now level 6, and mastered skills stay mastered.
Skill levels show as a ten-segment gauge that warms from bronze to silver to gold, and shimmers in rainbow colours once mastered.
Battles face off across the screen's diagonal: monsters up on the left looking down at you, your party lower on the right looking back up at them, both lines centred.
The victory card shows EXP with a star and gold with coins, and what you found as little item pictures with counts, instead of a list of lines.
In battle every fighter with MP shows a blue MP bar under their HP bar, and pinned skill buttons are labelled with the skill's name (cut short with … if it's long) instead of its MP cost.
The world map is turned like the game's view, with a compass: north is up-left and east is up-right, so the road you take off the top-right of the screen leads to the place up-right on the map.
Bars use the same colours everywhere: HP red, MP blue, EXP green. Battle HP bars were green, and your companion's HP bar on the map was orange.

Handing in a quest opens a Quest complete card like the victory card after a battle: EXP with a star, gold with coins, items as little pictures, plus any new looks and roads it opens. If it levels you up, the skill card follows.

New Monster Book (Companions → Monster Book): every monster you meet in battle is written down, with its lore, element (and what it's strong against and weak to), stats at the level you met it, skills, where it lives, rare drops and how many you've beaten. Monsters you haven't met yet show as dark silhouettes; filter the book by element.
Monsters of the same kind in one battle are just called by their name, without the A, B, C after it.

releases.title: Clean corner
notes: The four menu buttons on the map (Character, Companions, Bag, Quests) are icons only now, without the text underneath.
The title screen card is tidier: the hero's name and the companion line are gone (Continue already says who you are), leaving the hero and companion with your class, level and map.

releases.title: Light and strings
notes: New spells of light. Mages learn Recovery (Lv 10, heal an ally), Bridge of Light (Lv 20), Revive (Lv 35, wake a fainted ally mid-battle) and Bless (Lv 45, +25% strength and defense for 3 turns, more at higher levels). Tamers learn Revive at Lv 30, to bring a fainted companion back.
Bridge of Light is cast from the Character screen outside battle: tap Cast to be carried back to your last checkpoint.
The party heal Blessing is now called Healing Spring, like the original spell.
Wooden Puppets and the Marionette King look like real marionettes now, strings and all, instead of recoloured skeletons.
Tapping the minimap opens the world map only. The full map of the area you're in no longer shows, so caves and forests stay a mystery until you explore them.

releases.title: Signs and smiles
notes: Roads out of a map have a wooden signpost again. Walk up to it (a ? shows when you're close) and tap it to read where the road goes; tapping from afar walks you over first.
The title screen shows your hero facing you and breathing like they do in the game, with your companion close beside them doing its own idle bounce or sway.
The loading bar matches its percentage, and it learns how long each part of a map takes on your phone, so it fills at the real pace from the second visit on.
Hits in battle burst into a small fireball (hot core, flames, embers and a puff of smoke) instead of a cartoon star; critical hits blaze bigger, splash hits smaller, and heals glow green.

releases.title: Watch it fill
notes: Loading screens show a blue bar with a percentage instead of a spinner. The map is built a piece at a time behind it, so the bar moves as the ground, scenery, buildings and people go up.
In battle, names are smaller and sit right on top of each fighter's HP bar, so the field isn't covered in big labels.
Tap a quest in the Quests list to see its reward: gold, EXP, items with their icons, new looks and roads it opens. Tap a completed quest to see what it said and what you earned.
The title screen shows your active companion walking beside your hero.

releases.title: Tidy buttons
notes: Battle buttons sit in neat rows beside the big button instead of a tall column over your party, with More on top of the big button.
Pinned skills are round like the other battle buttons, with their MP cost underneath.

Rearranging works like the iPhone home screen: hold any battle button and they all wiggle. Drag one over another to take its place, onto the big button to make it the big one, or into the "Behind More" tray. Tap Done when you're happy.

releases.title: Back on the road
notes: Fixed: the game could crash while loading a map. Drawing the minimap's colours took so long on big maps that iOS stopped the app.
Deleting a game moved off the title screen, where its little × looked like it only closed the notice. It's now under Settings → Danger zone inside the game, and asks before deleting.

releases.title: Quieter streets
notes: Names step aside: your hero's and companions' names hide while you walk and come back when you stop.
Everyone else's name shows only when you walk up to them or tap them.
Arrange your battle buttons: hold any of them, then drag them into the order you like. The top one becomes the big button, so Attack can make way for a skill, and anything can go behind More.

releases.title: Glory in numbers
notes: Bigger battles: monster groups grow as you travel, from one to three in the first fields to as many as ten in the far lands, lined up in two rows.

Upgraded skills feel it: from level 2 your hero gathers power first, at 3 and 4 the hit bursts with rings, light rays and falling sparkles, and a mastered skill (level 5) blazes in gold with its name across the screen.
Class skills are spread over the long climb: new ones open at levels 15 to 70 instead of all before 30.
Play several heroes: a new game gets its own save, and the title screen lets you swipe between your games (and delete old ones).
The title screen shows each hero as they look in the game: race, hairstyle, colours and armour.
The quest list shows who gave you each quest, with their face and where they live, so you know where to report back.
Your hero walks on the Character screen and the title screen, turning to show every side.

releases.title: Within reach
notes: Battle buttons sit in one column right beside Attack: More at the bottom, Skills above it, and Capture, Items and your pinned skills stacking on top.
Your hero's name and gender are set for good when you create them; Customize still changes hairstyle and colours.
The minimap takes its colours from the map itself, so a purple wood or a snowy field looks the part.
Fixed light corners around the edge of the screen on moody maps like Twilight Woods.

releases.title: Into the mist
notes: Fixed a crash when continuing a game saved before 0.2.0 with friends in it.
The land beyond each map's edge now fades into a soft mist (a deep gloom in caves) instead of black.
A companion that faints stays down after the battle: it sits out fights and stops following you until a potion or a healer wakes it up, and earns no EXP from that fight.
Fixed the intro's first page running off the screen.

releases.title: A bigger Storyleaf
notes: The world grows to 30 maps, with a world atlas, winding roads, caves, snowfall, icy ponds and busier towns.
Levels now run to 105 and beyond, and you join a guild at level 10.
Three new bosses: Grumpy Old Oak, Great Wisp and the Moon Rabbit Queen. Bosses can be fought again, and six of them may drop a rare colour of their armour.
Choose male, female or other and a hairstyle. Helmets and hoods now cover your hair, and stronger armour shows finer detail.
Every item and skill has its own art, magic weapons glow, and blacksmiths forge gear from monster materials.
Battles show names above each fighter with level and HP below; the map shows faces for you, your companion and your party.
A storybook soundtrack, new sound effects with volume settings, an intro for new heroes and a What's new list.
Friends you've made turn up around the world now and then, and can only join your party when they're nearby.

releases.title: First steps into Storyleaf
notes: 14 maps joined by winding roads: Meadowbrook, Prismhaven and Ingothold, plus wild zones from Sunny Meadow to Moonwhisper.
Random encounters and turn-based battles fought where you stand. Big spells splash onto nearby monsters.
81 monsters across seven elements, with rare colour variants and three bosses.
Capture with Seal Stones and keep up to 5 companions. Your first hatches from the starter egg.
Start as a Novice and join a guild at level 5. Spend skill points to learn and power up skills.
Villagers and adventurers wander and chat. Befriend adventurers and bring two along in your party.
Customise hair, outfit and skin. Armour recolours your outfit and your weapon shows in hand.
Quests, shops, healers, checkpoints, an in-game calendar and a chiptune soundtrack.
